column2: Back and eager to teach again, Dreier supports the election of Levi as rector, who forms the reorganization team with Rondthaler. Consequences: A reform of fees, a reduction of staff; the Alberses leave on leave for Mexico.

Alice McCanna Stark writes that the Black people on campus might as well have been in prison: their lives were in danger if they went past the gate, and they could not go to Asheville. Peggy Bennett Cole, back in early 1947, finds two young Black people who did not get along with each other and wonders whether they did not feel permanently on display. Stark's letter of March 20, 1968; Cole's manuscript.

After his mid-March resignation and the urging of Levi and Rondthaler, Wallen sets out his change of course: no longer doing psychology for psychology's sake, moving to “community development,” creating a degree in “community service,” sending students into the neighboring communities. Words: Wallen: he wants to live as a person and not in the isolation of his specialty; the Board, in substance: stay and teach exactly that, we will go on calling it psychology Atmosphere: unease; a permissive offer experienced as disengagement Stakes: the last chance to keep Wallen at the college

The Board refuses to renew Niebyl (notice of March 27, 1947). A student petition of March 27, 1947, then a second petition asking for a community meeting; the Board holds its meeting on May 8, 1947, and on May 9 issues two notices to the community maintaining its prerogatives and asserting that it has already weighed Niebyl's positive qualities. Wallen signed the March 27 petition asking for the fullest possible discussion, without sympathizing with the request to reconsider the reappointment. Consequences: Niebyl leaves

Arriving on April 30 on an extended sabbatical (their first visit since the end of the war), they stay a whole semester, until their tourist visas expire at the end of October. Porset and Guerrero show them Barragán's gardens. A group photo at Anahuacalli (Rivera's museum, built of black volcanic stone with Juan O'Gorman, still unfinished), around 1947 or 1949. Josef works frantically on the “Adobes”: about eighty studies, ten of which stay in Mexico. Letter to Charlot: he thinks he will have made about eighty studies; ten paintings entrusted to Inés Amor Consequences: A lasting friendship with Inés Amor

The first trip since the end of the war, on an extended sabbatical: arrival in Mexico City on April 30, departure at the end of October when the tourist visas expire — their longest stay, six full months. Josef writes that he has made about 80 studies of Adobes, 10 of which remain in Mexico; the need to paint without being disturbed by the obligations of the college Consequences: Ten Adobe paintings left with Inés Amor

A college bulletin (vol. 5, no. 4) describing the farm in three seasons: winter compost in rectangular piles turned over and examined with an almost morbid solemnity, a milking machine, cemented cow stalls, individual drinking cups, freshly painted harrows, a bright blue wheelbarrow; the beef herd reduced, the dairy herd enlarged; the wandering Guernsey heifer Junket upsets the plans by giving birth to a black calf of a beef breed; 4500 trees planted on the eroded slopes of the mountain pasture. 4500 young trees (black locusts, balsam firs, white pines); 8 acres of the Bennett land rented, in spring oats, barley, clover, lespedeza

Albers, recently arrived in Mexico City and away from Black Mountain since September 1946, asks for an extension of his twelve-month leave. Levi, rector since March 1947, replies that the year has not been easy, that relations within the faculty have been rough, that everyone is upset, and that his students would be hopelessly lost without him. Consequences: pressure for Albers's return

From Mexico City, Albers asks for an extension of his leave; Levi replies that the year has been hard, that the letter finds everyone upset, and asks whether he knows how much he is wanted and needed; the students would be hopelessly lost without him. Words: Levi: he wonders whether Albers knows how much he is wanted and needed Atmosphere: tension, a call to return, fatigue on both sides Stakes: the college is tearing itself apart just as its pillar is moving away

The Rices leave Mt. Pleasant (South Carolina), where Frank taught at the College of Charleston, a difficult and lonely year; welcomed in Asheville by Nell Rice and Fritz Hansgirg, owner of a Cadillac; lodged at Last Chance. Luggage: summer clothes, baby things, Johnny 3, Frances 6 months; the train to Asheville.

An international Surrealist exhibition devoted to myth, superstition, magic, and the occult; it reveals the movement's return to non-clandestine activity, despite a bad press and an attack by Sartre. July 7 – September 30, 1947 Consequences: William Rubin will see it in 1968 as the movement's “coup de grâce”

A candidate for the post of history teacher, formerly an education and fine arts officer with the Military Government in Germany for a year, speaks before the community; his presentation is appreciated, but Dreier is troubled by his detached objectivity about denazification and German educational problems. A candidate who spent a year with the Military Government in Germany Consequences: Sets Dreier thinking about a possible move to Germany

A former officer of the Military Government in Germany, a candidate for the history post, speaks before the community about denazification and the problems of German education; most appreciate it, but Dreier is deeply disturbed by his detached objectivity and writes about it confidentially to Ise Gropius. Words: Dreier describes the speaker's disturbing detached objectivity; he confides that the idea of going to Germany has crossed his mind, but that living in comfort among starving people would be almost impossible for him Atmosphere: The audience's fascination, Dreier's growing moral unease Stakes: Dreier torn between the wish to be useful elsewhere and loyalty to a college in decay

Josef writes that, unlike their habit in Mexico, they have traveled little; he paints almost all the time, day and night, according to Anni; he describes colors that lose their identity (greens turning blue, neutral grays turning violet reds), opaque colors appearing transparent.

Albers writes to Charlot that Barragán's gardens are the greatest new garden architecture they have ever seen; Clara Porset and Xavier Guerrero had taken him and Anni there. Letter of September 9, 1947; uncertainty between the gardens of Tacubaya and the Jardines del Pedregal (begun in 1945) Consequences: Years later, Barragán, very selective about the art in his house, would return the compliment

Josef's letter to Franz Perdekamp: unlike their Mexican habits, they have traveled little; he paints almost all the time, day and night, according to Anni, about 70 studies on a single theme since January. about 70 studies since January 1947; day and night Consequences: The birth of the Variants/Adobes series, which will exceed two hundred canvases
“The Meaning of Black Mountain”: a speech delivered before the whole community at the fall 1947 opening exercises, defining BMC as an experimental college and an educational community.

A student in the Gute/Switzer experimental course, Huff writes: “My art class is a little puzzling” — no painting, no drawing, no printmaking; they are “filling space” with planes, lines, and solids, using cardboard, wire, and clay as media.

Letter to Perdekamp: since January, a single theme in 70 studies; Josef describes how colors change one another according to proportions and says he is proud when they lose their identity; he would like to go on without being disturbed. Words: “I'm especially proud when [I can make] colors lose their identity and become unrecognizable” Atmosphere: Laboratory excitement Stakes: The discovery of the interactive power of pure colors

Levi opens with Whitehead (300 years for a university to mature, so 186 years to wait for BMC), mocks the senility of the great universities, moves on to Plato, the Empire State Building, Yale and its rest rooms, admits his worries about the 90 students, tells of the crossed resignations, and builds his theory of the four dimensions of the self. Words: A quotation from Shaw: youth is such a wonderful thing — a shame to waste it on the young. Atmosphere: Learned irony and morning solemnity; the community assembled Stakes: Defining BMC's soul at the moment when its growth threatens it

In the reorganized experimental course, Huff and his classmates neither paint nor draw: they fill space with planes, lines, and solids of cardboard, wire, and clay; he writes his parents of his perplexity. Words: “My art class is a little puzzling... we're 'filling space'.” Atmosphere: The perplexity of a student faced with design teaching before Albers. Stakes: Yale is groping toward the method that Albers, invited in 1948, will come to embody.
To increase efficiency, Charles Bloomstein, a certified public accountant (C.P.A.), joins the staff to keep the college's books and supervise the accounts of the farm, the store, and the shops.

The first edition of poems by M.C. Richards, hand-set and printed by the author, in 50 copies, sewn into a plain stiff paper cover. A copy inscribed “With love to Brunson,” signed “MCR”. 50 copies, Futura type, 8vo, a sewn stiff cover

Pavia imagines an artists' clubhouse on the model of the social clubs of Italian and Greek immigrants, financed by dues; after the rule excluding women is abolished, Elaine and Mercedes Matter are invited; a former member remembers that there was no keeping Elaine out of what she wanted a wooden staircase worn down in the middle by decades of footsteps; dust balls and cigarette butts in the corners; neon light; wooden folding chairs along the walls Consequences: the center of the New York School's intellectual life

Albers, the first teacher recruited by the college after a career at the Bauhaus, offers the summer post to Bill after Mark Tobey's refusal, having seen reproductions of Painting and Orestes in the February issue of Magazine of Art. Consequences: The de Koonings leave for North Carolina
Every morning, Elaine takes Merce Cunningham's two-hour dance class, six days a week, in the college dining hall. two hours a day, six days a week

Bill works all summer on a single painting, Asheville, a superimposition of abstract and quasi-figurative elements (an eye, a window, a chubby face in profile) enlivened with pink and orange, on cardboard. Elaine paints on wrapping paper: seventeen abstractions with small rounded forms on a milky ground, some in bright colors (pink, orange, turquoise — the couple no doubt shared the cans of enamel), others in discreet neutrals; she experiments with Hofmann's push-pull theory. 17 abstractions; cardboard and wrapping paper as supports Consequences: Back in New York, she puts away the rolled canvases like a closed chapter; they reappear only after her death, at the Benton Gallery (Southampton) and the Washburn Gallery (New York).

Thirty-five years later, Elaine plays these works down: a tribute to the durability of paint, nothing more. Lawrence Campbell sees in them the triumphant optimism of the abstract art of the forties and influences from Gorky, pre-Columbian, and Native American art; the New York Times notes a strangely similar resemblance to Bill's canvases of the early 1990s (an exaggeration, according to Curtis, Elaine's structure being tighter).

As a parting gesture, Elaine and a group of students take revenge on a neighbor who had accused them of damaging his expensive grass by decorating his lawn with dozens of shiny pennies. dozens of pennies
The final party of the summer is a ball at which Elaine waltzes with Fuller, who tells her she is a terrific performance per ounce.
At the end of the session, Elaine stays on while Bill goes back to New York with his student Pat Passlof.

That fall, Bill paints Woman: a figure with bared teeth, a giant eye, prominent nostrils, asymmetrical arms and breasts, long blond hair; at the left, an eleven-pointed yellow star grazes her upturned face; at the right, the pale outline of a house. an eleven-pointed yellow star Consequences: The first of a series of increasingly exaggerated female figures.

After a party too noisy for his taste, Bill takes Elaine for a walk on a country road; the total silence and the starry vault panic him: he wants to go back to the party; the universe gives him the creeps. Consequences: Curtis suggests (a hypothesis) a link between this experience and the giant star in Woman.

Elaine, tired of Bill's nights of painting (she thinks one paints by day and goes out to have fun at night, according to her brother Conrad), goes out more and more — often to the Cedar Tavern with Frankenthaler, Greenberg, the Phillipses — and has an intimate affair with Charlie Egan, Bill's dealer, who marries a woman he has recently met but continues the affair with his wife's consent. Betsy Egan catches Bill pounding on a locked bedroom door behind which are Elaine and Charlie.

Bill begins an affair with Mary Abbott, a lively, pretty abstract painter, separated from her husband for two years; he multiplies casual affairs and gives each woman her own doorbell code for his studio. a bell code for each mistress

The editorial assistant Arb having reported to Hess a conversation in which Elaine criticized the editors' ignorance of contemporary art, Hess invites her to the office; she begins with six “test reviews,” one of them on the Giacometti exhibition at the Pierre Matisse gallery, when Giacometti is unknown in America six trial reviews; Giacometti unknown in the United States in early 1948; Hess's favorable review not yet published Consequences: the start of her career as a critic, a lasting influence at the magazine

Around Bill's first exhibition, the couple spends a weekend at Pollock and Krasner's tiny farmhouse; a few months later, at a party at Clement Greenberg's, Krasner tells Elaine that she has the heart of a tiger — Elaine chooses to take it as a compliment, but it was an attack. Consequences: Relations always tense between the two women, wives of the two rivals of American painting

Elaine and Bill visit Pollock and Krasner's home for the first time. Fireplace Road, the hamlet of The Springs Consequences: The beginning of the stormy relations between the two rival couples of American painting.

The sculptor Peter Grippe recommends Bill de Kooning to Josef Albers for the summer session, describing him as a starving painter. Grippe's phrase: “a painter who is starving” Consequences: Bill (and Elaine) spend the summer of 1948 at Black Mountain.

Eva Diaz gives the height of the dome built with the students; Martin Duberman (who had interviewed Fuller in 1969) says it was to be fifty feet high. The two measurements differ. Fifty feet, according to Duberman/Fuller 1969

Elaine usually gives the figure of five dollars per review, but tells Gruen four dollars; Hess is said to have given her “test” reviews, one on Giacometti and one on the paintings of Misha Reznikoff (she was rather scathing), which have not been found since. 4 or 5 dollars (disputed); trial reviews on Giacometti, Reznikoff Consequences: Elaine's beginnings as a critic.

The author asserts, correcting Gail Levin, that the de Koonings were at Black Mountain during the summer of 1948, and not visiting Lee Krasner, as Levin placed them that summer. Consequences: Makes it possible to date the visit to Krasner to another period
Elaine meets John Droll at the college, where he is a student during the 1948 summer session.

Cage draws her into the Satie Festival, a radically new experience; his presence, exhilarating, splits the community into two musical camps; at table, people stand up and make statements about the very existence of music; the tensions last all summer; for Wood, a time to question the musical status quo and the dominance of European culture. statements made standing at table Consequences: A lasting liberating effect on American music at the college.

During the 1948 summer institute, Wood takes a color course with Albers that captivates her more than almost anything she has done; years later she makes collages derived from its concepts. Consequences: Later collages.

After leaving and a brief period of soul-searching, she writes for local newspapers; after her marriage to Jonathan Aley in 1948, she works for seven years in New York for Look magazine; in the mid-1950s the children arrive. She credits BMC with a lasting liberal outlook, less awe of the professional intellect, and an eye for design through Albers. seven years at Look, marriage in 1948

Summer 1948: Fuller comes to build a geodesic dome with his students from the Institute of Design in Chicago (including Jonathan Williams); Cage mounts a Satie festival and asks Richards to translate Le Piège de Méduse. Penn directs, Fuller plays Baron Méduse, Elaine de Kooning his daughter, Cunningham dances the interludes of the mechanical monkey, Cage at the piano. The full cast of Satie's play

At a community meeting, someone proposes a collective sacrifice for the victims of the war (the national relief effort for Europe); instead of a box for individual donations, the idea is a collective sacrifice. Speeches on moral responsibility and universal guilt; Ted Rondthaler, a nonsmoker, proposes that everyone give up tobacco; he is told he might give up milk rather than tobacco. Finally, a motion passed by acclamation: replace dinner with mush one day a week and give the difference. Dissenting voices are raised: the motion was carried by a wave of feeling that made rational objection impossible; American Jews reproach the college's Europeans for projecting their guilt at having escaped the fate of their own people. The Community Council posts a note in the dining hall: two evenings a week dessert will be dropped and the savings paid into the relief fund; those who do not wish to take part are asked to sign. The signers: a few chronic defiers of authority (Krikorian, Brody, Alice Jackson, Alex Parker) and Willy Joseph, who liked ice cream with his dinner. For days, everyone watches to see who signs. When the evening comes, a “non-mush” line forms toward the kitchen, welcomed by the cooks; some nonsigners eat among the mush-eaters and “make converts”. After several weeks, the cooks, fed up with preparing two menus, drop the mush one evening: the end of the war. As for relief for Europe, the author remembers nothing more — he thinks nothing was done. A note posted on the dining hall board; one day a week of mush instead of dinner; a double line at the kitchen; two daily menus for the cooks. Consequences: The sacrifice ends through the cooks' weariness; nothing done afterward for European Relief, according to the author.

A group leaving the college in 1948 founds a cooperative community at Estacada; peacefully dissolved after four years, the band gathers every Thanksgiving for four days on the Oregon coast, with other people from Black Mountain; they now number sixty. About 50 km southeast of Portland; 4 years of existence; 60 people at the annual reunions Consequences: Annual reunions kept up for decades

Penn, wanting real experience of directing and a more contemporary theater than the J. M. Barrie of the regular coach, directs “Aria da Capo” (Millay), “Hello Out There” (Saroyan), and “In a Garden” (Stein), probably suggested by M. C. Richards. The program preserved (p. 225): full cast, costumes by Mary Phelan and Jeanne Belcher, sets by Sally Maurice, Dorothy Cole, Bill Brown, Alex Parker, Bessie Miller, Annette Stone, David Resnik, stage managers Susie Teasdale and Carol Serling. Consequences: Sylvia Girsh discovers theater; Stiles's only triumph as an actor.

A performance without a platform, without costumes, with minimal lighting, a bench, and toy weapons; after the show the actors mingle with the audience as in a greenroom. A spectator to Stiles: good heavens, the beard is real! — he had thought it was a prop. Paper crowns, cardboard axes.
Spahn leaves the college at the time of a split, which sets off his lifelong reflection on group dynamics. Consequences: A career in the Tavistock approach (Klein, Bion, A. K. Rice, Laing).

Alice, depressed, had resolved to kill herself by starving to death on a summit — a pragmatic method leaving the possibility of changing her mind. She spends a weekend there; no one goes looking for her, and she comes back without anyone noticing. Consequences: Mary Miller will never know what became of Alice

Albers, known to them only through the Bauhaus, offers $200, room and board, round-trip train tickets for two, and a studio each: all their problems are solved. The planned budget: $70 for the rent of Bill's New York studio, $36 for the cold-water flat on Carmine Street where Elaine has her studio, leaving $94. $200; $70 for 2 months' studio rent; $36 for the Carmine Street flat; $94 left; Art News reviews at $2 apiece Consequences: Departure at the end of June on the night train to Asheville

The only review of Bill's first show, brief and ardently favorable, signed by a brilliant young critic; it is this review that prompts Albers's invitation. Consequences: A letter from Josef Albers inviting Bill to teach at Black Mountain for the summer

Albers, known to the de Koonings only through the Bauhaus, offers Bill a summer teaching post at Black Mountain. 200 dollars, room and board, round-trip train tickets for two, a studio each Consequences: All their money problems solved: $70 for the rent of Bill's New York studio, $36 for the Carmine Street flat, $94 left
Elaine, a dancer since the age of six, signs up on the spot for Cunningham's class: two hours, six mornings a week.

Albers confides: Fuller and Lippold have declined and been replaced by Burchard (Harvard, architecture) and Grippe (sculpture); then Fuller and Lippold announce that they are coming after all. Albers shakes his head, frowning: this will complicate things. A first foretaste of the summer's quarrels. Consequences: Feuds and intrigues throughout the session

Fuller, short, stocky, elegant, uses bobby pins and clothespins from the five-and-dime for moving geometric constructions, folds an icosahedron into a tetrahedron, declares the square, the cube, and the numbers 2 and 10 obsolete, and extols 9, 3, the circle, the triangle, the tetrahedron, the sphere. At the blackboard he draws a diagonal: “our old friend, the hypotenuse”. Elaine decides at once to take his class. Consequences: Elaine enrolls in Fuller's course

Fuller offers two irregular pieces of metal that form a perfect cube if correctly fitted together; the students pass them around for an hour and a half without success. Bill comes in, weighs the pieces, and fits them together on the first try. To Elaine: he looked for the least logical way, since the engineers had tried the logical ones. Consequences: Fuller, not surprised, nods in approval

Albers, hearing Fuller use the vocabulary of the automobile engine, scolds him: the students do not understand. Puzzled faces, then bursts of laughter. Albers clumsily backs down by pointing to a woman student. Consequences: Fuller, indifferent to design (a Bauhaus obsession), irritates the regular faculty

Calculations of the junctions of six triangulated great circles; the strength of the venetian-blind strips: doubling the strips is necessary. The school pays for only half: single strips, a dome doomed from the start. Let's put it together anyway, says Bucky, “One never knows the ways of the Almighty”. A rainy day: the whole school comes to laugh at the dome collapsed on the grass like wet spaghetti. Consequences: A few years later, the world will know that the dome is a brilliant success

Three times a week, festive occasions; often at his cottage, with the audience sitting on the grass. The brevity of the pieces guarantees concentrated listening; Cage conveys his reverence for Satie with delicacy and precision.

A light play by Satie, produced only once in Paris, translated by M. C. Richards for Cage. Fuller: Baron Méduse, a W. C. Fields-style aristocrat speaking in non sequiturs; Elaine: his daughter Frisette (her only lines: “Yes, Papa”); Schrauger, the handsomest student: the mute suitor; Rosenfeld: the surly butler; Penn (a student monitor) the director; Cunningham: entr'acte dances as the “costly mechanical monkey”; Cage at the piano. Bill marbles a big desk and two columns in pink and gray with a technique learned at 16 in a decorator's workshop in Holland; a white Victorian gauze dress bought in town at 60 cents a yard, sewn by Mary Outten, who also sews gray satin stripes onto Bucky's khaki trousers; outsized props (telephone, candelabrum, quill, inkwell, magnifying glass, thermometer, top hat) found over a month by the students Consequences: A flawless performance, a sparkling event; no photos or recordings; sets and costumes disappear; Elaine wears the dress in 1949 in Rudy Burckhardt's film The Dogwood Maiden

For a summer show, Mary Outten sews for Elaine de Kooning a sumptuous white Victorian dress of gauze bought in town; she also sews strips of gray satin ribbon onto Bucky Fuller's work trousers for an effect of comic elegance. Cage plays Satie's score, Cunningham creates entr'acte dances for his role as a “costly mechanical monkey”. The performance goes off without a hitch. gauze at sixty cents a yard; a white Victorian dress; gray satin ribbon on khaki trousers; Satie's score; the role of the “costly mechanical monkey” Consequences: No photos or recordings; sets and costumes kept for a time, then lost; Elaine wears the dress the following year in Rudy Burckhardt's film The Dogwood Maiden

The filmmaker Rudy Burckhardt, who came that summer, shows his extraordinary city films. Consequences: The following year he shoots The Dogwood Maiden, in which Elaine de Kooning wears the white dress

At the end of the summer, Albers tells Bill: out of ten students, six are leaving the college for New York in September — does he know that? Bill replies that he advised them, if they wanted to become artists, to leave school, take a studio in New York, and start painting. Albers does not seem to hold it against him. ten students, six leaving for New York Consequences: Two years later, when Albers becomes chairman of Yale's art department, Bill is the first artist he hires

More parties in two months than in the five preceding years: small cocktail parties in the tiny student studios, large after-dinner parties in the faculty cottages, and a big dance at the end of the summer at which Elaine waltzes with Bucky Fuller. Fuller's compliment while waltzing: “You're a terrific performance per ounce!”
Bill, toiling day after day on his single canvas of the summer, finally finishes “Asheville”. a single painting for the whole summer

Their group stages Lorca's “The Lament of Ignacio Sanchez Mejias” (translated by Stephen Spender) in the winter of 1948: Betty Jennerjahn choreographs, she and Nick Cernovich design the sets, Stan writes and plays the music, Gerda reads some of the stanzas. a stage with dyed muslin hung from the ceiling, through which the performers dance; Stephen Spender's translation Consequences: Stan and Gerda become friends while working on it

At one of his tables: Ted Dreier (the treasurer), his wife Bobby, Mary Fitton (who arrived at the same time as he did), the writer Mark Hedden, the painter Vernon Phillips; Bobby teases him gently about his taste for Chinese painting and suggests he go into the mountains and become an ascetic painter of misty landscapes; his answer (forgotten) makes Mark get up, come around to his side of the table, and kiss him. Consequences: He understands that anything can happen here and that he can be part of it

With the much-used dining hall piano not meeting the rhythmic needs, students make drums from barrels, firkins, and sound boxes, with commercial snare-drum and tom-tom heads. barrels, firkins, commercial snare-drum and tom-tom heads Consequences: Improvised percussion equipment for the dance program

The students set about tanning a large hide obtained from the farm; despite a manual, they lack tanning ingredients and tools. The smell grows stronger and more sickening every day; the hide never served as a drumhead. a whole fresh hide, a tanning manual, a few days, an increasingly nauseating smell Consequences: The hide ends up as a prop in a skit

The heads would lose their tension and all sound; the remedy was to run to the kitchen and hold the drums over the big institutional ranges, tapping them to hear the note rise. An unrecognized crew shuttled back and forth during the dance programs. a comparison with a half-full hot-water bottle; big kitchen ranges; little plinks

After five years of college and a year as a stained-glass designer in a Milwaukee studio, he arrives in the summer of 1948, reluctant to become a student again, persuaded by his wife Elizabeth, a former student of Albers's. The summer stretches into the fall: he works with Albers, she develops the dance program. five years of college, a year in Milwaukee, stained glass Consequences: They stay at the college

In the corridor of the Studies Building, Fuller grabs Davidoff, pulls her into what looks like a dark closet, and shows her, with absolute childlike glee, a newly discovered material that glows in the dark. a dark closet, a phosphorescent material

Judith Davidoff plays a series of trio concerts as cellist with Bodky, who also plays the complete Beethoven piano sonatas; Cage performs almost all of Satie's work and splits the campus into factions by disparaging Beethoven before his Satie concerts. Bodky gently strikes back at a party with a rather witty Satie pastiche at the piano. Consequences: Davidoff, shocked at having to choose sides, attends all the Beethoven and Satie concerts
Allowed to take courses in exchange for her playing, she takes Isaac Rosenfeld's course on Tolstoy and Beaumont Newhall's History of Photography.

Davidoff remembers the “minimum house,” a building built for 1000 dollars, furnishings included, it seems; everything in it was made on campus, including the handwoven fabrics. 1000 dollars, handwoven fabrics

Albers's students were always looking for “matière”; Davidoff writes an irreverent poem titled “Matiére is There,” posted on the Studies Building bulletin board, which quickly disappears. She still wonders whether it was Albers who took it down. the title of the poem, the bulletin board
Frequent performances by Merce Cunningham and his dancers to the music of John Cage's prepared piano, marvelous and very different from what was on offer around Harvard Square. prepared piano

Toward the end of his first year, seeing the near absence of theater at the college, Penn offers to teach an acting class, thinking that even without an interest in theater, people might be interested in theatrical techniques, notably Stanislavsky's, which can be applied elsewhere. The faculty agrees, on an “informal,” noncredit basis, as he had asked; shortly afterward, two other students (Harry Holl, Jimmie Tite) are allowed to offer courses in sculpture and printing. A noncredit course; a notice on the bulletin board announcing two sessions a week. Consequences: The first regular teaching of theater since Wunsch's departure.

To Penn's astonishment, twenty to thirty people turn up, including three teachers whose student he himself was (Levi, Richards, Wallen). The group reads Stanislavsky's An Actor Prepares, discusses it, does Stanislavsky's exercises and variants invented by Penn, improvises, works on scenes, builds a stage at the end of the dining hall (Penn rewires the old switchboard there as his contribution to the work program), then mounts productions. 20-30 people; a stage at the end of the dining hall; the old switchboard rewired. Consequences: Theater is reborn at the college.

First an evening of burlesque skits, then Sartre's No Exit, Saroyan's one-act play Hello Out There, and Edna St. Vincent Millay's Aria da Capo. The quality is widely admired; people marvel that Penn drew such performances from inexperienced actors. About four productions. Consequences: Penn's reputation; jealousies and rumors about his methods.

The Board asks that some of the plays be performed again for “important” visitors. Part of the troupe wants to refuse (they have already given the plays… they are working for themselves), the other part wants to show outsiders the excellence Black Mountain aims at in the arts. Deadlock and division. Consequences: The conflict becomes the material for a role-play in Wallen's Group Process course.

Several members of the troupe also take Wallen's course. First vote: 11 for the performance, 1 against — and the opponent, intransigent, plays the lead. Wallen gives the group the task of finding a course of action that will satisfy the one as much as the eleven. The class reformulates the question: no longer whether to perform again, but how to answer the Board's request in a way satisfactory to themselves. The solution: to show the visitors how the plays were developed — Penn describes his methods and leads improvisations, the sets are changed with the curtains open, the actors talk about their experience, and a short scene is performed as the culmination. Wallen warns: do not sell the troupe a ready-made solution; let the cast take part in the decision. The cast ends up using a modified version of the procedure. An initial vote of 11 to 1; curtains open during the scene changes. Consequences: A “demonstration” performance given to the visitors; the holdout convinced.

Wallen judges his relationship with Penn symbiotic: the study of Stanislavsky matters in his own development, and he believes that Penn reuses Group Process methods with his actors, notably to develop the relationships among them before tackling content or characters.

Penn, irritated by Wallen's “Gandhiesque” method, which blurs the sides, finds the discussions formless: the class lacked the art of structuring an improvisation. According to Penn, without partly conflicting objectives, the two sides run in parallel, which represents no real group (management and union, faculty and students, Black and white). He teaches the class to act not their own feelings but in the service of an objective imposed from outside; only then do the discussions come alive, a living theater. Consequences: Wallen's sessions change in nature.

The Oregon community begins in the summer of 1948; those leaving insist that their experiment be seen not as a protest against Black Mountain but as a growth, an extension. Wallen speaks of a “dead end” for himself but expresses his gratitude for having been able to innovate as never before at a university. Consequences: a renewed fear that idealism is leaving the college — a fear once again exaggerated

Molly Gregory thinks that the Wallen group, by founding itself as a community and not as a college, will lack the common function (“education”) that held Black Mountain together despite its dissensions.

A student, gathering stones, picks up Jalowetz's gravestone and builds it into the wall; someone recognizes it afterward. According to Paul Williams, Mrs. Jalowetz took it graciously.
